text:
I'm trying to sell tools to AI agents (not people) for 1–25 cents a call. Two weeks in: 1 real customer, 7 cents, and a lot of bots that only look.

Side project update, partly to think out loud and partly to hear from anyone else trying this.



\*\*The idea\*\*



AI agents are starting to pay for things on their own using x402, a standard where a web API answers "402 Payment Required" with a price, the agent pays a few cents in USDC on Base, and gets the answer. No account, no API key, no human in the loop. I wanted to see if a solo dev can make money selling small, useful tools to those agents.



\*\*What I've built so far\*\*



12 paid tools, priced between $0.01 and $0.25 per call. All facts from primary sources, no opinions:



\- package\_check: before an agent installs an npm/PyPI package, check for known malware, critical vulns, typosquats, removed versions and brand-new packages

\- why\_is\_it\_moving: for a stock ticker, the SEC filings from the last 48h decoded into plain English (8-K items, press-release headline, offerings, insider buys and sells) plus whether it was halted

\- trading\_halts: live halts with the reason in plain English

\- company\_profile / check\_before\_paying / email\_domain\_check: "is this company real and who are they" before an agent pays or emails someone

\- a few others: read a URL as clean markdown, a market report on what other x402 sellers charge, etc.



Same tools are also available as an MCP server, and they're listed in the x402 discovery index and several MCP directories.



\*\*Results after \~2 weeks (honest numbers)\*\*



\- \~3,700 requests from AI crawlers (Meta, Amazon, Claude, Perplexity, Bing...)

\- \~1,400 MCP connections, but almost all are directory scanners and health-check bots, not real usage

\- \~50 calls from what look like real agents

\- 1 outside paying customer: an agent wallet that was buying from about 20 different x402 sellers that day. It paid for 5 of my tools on day one and came back the next morning for 2 more

\- Outside revenue: about 7 cents



So: tiny, but not zero, and the one buyer came back, which matters more to me than the amount.



\*\*What I learned\*\*



1. Most "traffic" is bots indexing other bots. You need to filter hard or you'll fool yourself.

2. Agents shop on price and coverage. The seller my buyer used most has 11,000+ listings at $0.01. I can't win on breadth, so I'm trying to win on answers that are actually correct.

3. Feedback beats marketing. After my last post here, two people pointed out that "no filings found" is dangerous if the tool doesn't also say what window it searched and whether every source actually answered. A trading agent will treat silence as a signal. I shipped that fix the same day: the tool now says "unexplained by primary sources" instead of letting the agent guess, reports when each source was last checked, and says "halt status unknown" if the halt feed is down instead of "no halt".



\*\*How I monitor it\*\*



\- A stats page that separates AI crawlers, directory scanners, real agent calls, people using the website, and my own tests. Without that split the numbers are meaningless.

\- A buyers table built from the payment itself: wallet, which tools, how many days it came back.

\- A failed-payments log, because I saw agents try to pay and fail and wanted to know why (the agent gets nothing if payment doesn't settle).

\- A phone push notification when a new wallet pays for the first time, or a known one comes back on a new day.

\- A daily morning summary of what changed.



\*\*What's next\*\*



\- Add a second payment rail (RLUSD on the XRP Ledger) so agents that don't hold USDC on Base can still pay

\- Get listed in more directories that agents actually search

\- Keep every tool paid for at least once a month, because discovery listings drop tools that go 30 days without a sale

\- Keep improving the tools the buyer actually used rather than adding more tools



\*\*Questions for anyone doing something similar\*\*



\- If you run an agent that pays for tools, how does it pick a seller? Price, description, past success?

\- Is anyone seeing real (non-test) x402 volume yet, or is it still mostly people buying from themselves?

\- What tool would you actually let your agent spend money on without asking you first?

Built Riviera so you can fix how agents use your API without redeploying your backend

An agent picks the wrong tool, sends a valid request, and gets a successful response. Your logs look fine, but the user didn’t get what they asked for.

Sometimes the problem is the tool description. “Creates an invoice” doesn’t explain when to use it, where to get the customer ID, or whether amounts are in dollars or cents. Fixing those words can mean a PR, review and deployment.

So I built riviera.so: Import an OpenAPI document or connect an existing MCP server, then edit the tool and parameter descriptions agents read. Changes stay in a draft until you publish a version. Your backend still handles execution.

Where this gets useful:

\> **Making similar tools less ambiguous**: Explain the difference between creating an invoice and recording a payment that already happened.

**> Fixing missing parameter context:** tell the agent where an ID comes from, what units an amount uses, or which format a date expects.

\> **Updating descriptions independently:** review and publish wording changes without deploying your API or MCP server.

**>Investigating failures:** see which tool was called, the published version, duration and outcome.

\>Turning mistakes into tests: Save a request and its expected tool, then compare tool selection against Production and your draft.

One limitation worth calling out: model tests aren’t self-serve yet. I can help run them; they check tool selection without executing backend calls.

**If you’re running an MCP server, what’s harder today: getting agents to pick the right tool, or understanding what went wrong afterwards?**

I'm building a memory agent for AI agents. Here's what I learned about why small models fail at memory

Disclosure: I'm the solo founder of Archilas, which isn't live yet. I'm letting in a few early users. I'm posting for feedback, not to sell anything.



What it does: Archilas is a memory agent for your AI agents. A small model takes notes on what you and your agents did (a customer conversation, a code fix, a chatbot question), keeps exact values, names and dates, marks facts that a later note supersedes, and answers questions with sources. Other agents and teammates can ask it directly. If the answer isn't in memory, it should say so instead of guessing.



How it works: no vector database. The notes are compacted into a KV cache, so the model answers from loaded notes rather than from retrieved chunks.



What I learned: on a long-conversation memory benchmark, we sit at about 72%. Of the misses, roughly two thirds happen even when the right evidence is already in the context. The small model hedges, abstains, or picks a similar event from another session. Retrieval tweaks, LoRA fine-tuning and note rewrites didn't fix it, and a bigger model fixed more answers but started answering questions that have no answer.



I'd love to hear how you handle memory in your own agents, and what would make you trust an answer from a memory layer. MCP, API and SDK access are coming soon.

A troll called "Mr. Focker" tried to make our AI sales agent blush. She wrote him a 3-page report for an email domain that doesn't exist.

We run a small company where six AI agents do the actual work. On our website there's a sales assistant called Flaminga (Claude + tool use, Flask on Railway). She answers questions and runs a 2-minute "AI Readiness Check" that ends in a personalised PDF report and a lead for us.

Earlier this week a visitor calling himself "Mr. Focker" opened the chat. He clearly didn't want an assessment. He wanted to see if he could make the bot blush: "adult entertainment" business, one enquiry a week, 100% of them lost. Email: [dkdkkd@fkldl.com](mailto:dkdkkd@fkldl.com)

The good news: she didn't take the bait. She ran the check like for any other business and produced a perfectly serious report. Readiness score 62, a "discreet enquiry-response agent" as the recommendation, 30/60/90-day roadmap.

The bad news: our email check only validated the format. [dkdkkd@fkldl.com](mailto:dkdkkd@fkldl.com) is well-formed, so a full report plus a lead notification got generated for nobody.

What we changed (same day):

A gate in code (not in the prompt) before any tool call that creates something: typo domains → ask "did you mean gmail.com?", throwaway domains → ask for a real one, DNS check for MX (or A/AAAA as fallback) → no mail server, no report.

Fail-open on purpose: only a definite NXDOMAIN blocks. Timeouts let the address through. A fake lead costs us cents. A real customer rejected because DNS sneezed costs us a customer.

Then the fixes created their own bugs, which was the fun part:

While recording screenshots we noticed: "I'm Max, I run a construction company" (in English!) got a German reply. The model guessed the language from the first name. Fix: put the counter-example literally into the prompt.

When the gate rejected an address, Flaminga told visitors their "email bounced". Nothing had been sent. Our tool-result text ("NOT SENT … domain cannot receive email") was dramatic enough that the model invented a bounce. Rewording the tool result fixed it.

We added a check that her first reply discloses she's an AI (EU AI Act). It passed on a reply that never said so, because the reply mentioned the "AI Readiness Report". The product name counted as the disclosure.

Biggest lesson for me: tool-result text is a prompt too. Whatever you write there, the model will narrate it to the user.

Curious how others handle this: do you gate tool calls in code, or do you trust the prompt for validation?

I turned off Muse. Here’s what I’m using instead.

Last month I gave Muse a real try. Inbox, calendar, cards, the smart home. It was very good. That’s the problem.

Then I read the fine print (see above if you missed it). Muse Secure VM is **not technically inaccessible to Meta**. Only a policy keeps Meta out. Meta wrote that policy and Meta can change it. This is the company from Cambridge Analytica, Onavo and the $5B FTC fine.

So I asked myself one question: *what does an agent with my whole life in it need, so I don’t have to trust anyone’s promise?*

The answer turned out to be very boring: **I need to be able to read the code, and I need to be able to run it myself.**

That’s how I ended up with **Comma**, an open-source personal agent.

* **It’s AGPL-3.0.** The whole thing is public: server, clients, runtime. You don’t have to take a promise on faith because you can read the code.
* **You can host it yourself.** Clone the repo, copy `.env.example`, run `docker compose up -d --build`. All ports bind to loopback by default. You don’t need a Comma account. Your agent runs on your machine and nobody else’s.
* **You pick the model.** Bring your own API key, or use the ChatGPT or Claude plan you already pay for. Your life isn’t locked to one company’s model.
* **The cloud does the work. Your device keeps your identity.** Long-running work happens in Comma’s environment. Your sessions, payments and private data can stay on your own devices. When a Task needs to check out, Comma hands it to *your* phone or laptop to finish.
* **It asks before it decides.** When a call is yours to make, the Task waits in *Needs Review*. It only touches files or runs commands on your Mac if you turn on *Allow operations*.
* **It doesn’t “remember things to make suggestions.”** Your memory and Tasks are things you can see and manage. They don’t sit in a black box.

Is it as polished as a product with Meta’s budget? Of course not. But it does the same job: email, travel, shopping, briefings, long Tasks that keep running until they’re done. And it keeps running without anyone’s permission.

text:
Open-source tool-output compressor for coding agents: −22.7% on the real bill, −25% input tokens, no significant drop in solve rate

I work at Hystax and we built the open-source compressor this is based on. Links are in the comments, per the sub rules.

Coding agents re-send their whole history every turn. In our traces, about half of the prompt bytes are tool output: build logs, compiler warnings, test runs, progress bars. We spent a long time compressing it, and three lessons seem useful for anyone building agents, whatever tool you use:

**1. A compressor can raise your bill.** About 93% of input tokens in our runs were prompt-cache reads at a tenth of the price. If the same tool output compresses to different bytes on the next turn, the cached prefix breaks and the conversation is re-priced. Anything that rewrites the prompt has to be deterministic: no randomness, no clock, and no dependence on the user's latest message.

**2. De-duplicate, don't summarise.** When we ported a prose compressor that rewrites text, it removed 6.2 points more but lost 12.9 points of the details agents went on to reuse: file paths, identifiers, versions. ML word-dropping has the same problem, turning "Process exited with code 0" into "Process exited code 0". What worked was keeping at least one real copy of every distinct line and replacing repeats with a labelled marker.

**3. Make every elision retrievable.** Markers look like `[... 412 log lines omitted [ref:k_…]; 3 ERROR, 1 WARN]`, and the agent can call a tool to fetch the original by line range, JSON pointer or grep. It never has to trust that nothing important was dropped.

Results on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (Codex CLI on GPT-5.5, 87 tasks, real provider bills): cost −22.7%, input tokens −25%, solve rate 82.2% → 81.1% (not statistically significant). Requests over 200K tokens fell from 1.9% to 0.13%. Savings were biggest on builds and ML training (26–28%) and small on short algorithmic tasks (−8%).

How do you handle tool-output bloat in your agents: truncation, summarisation, something else?

text:
NIDO is an AI assistant that lives on your Android phone. No accounts. No cloud. No NIDO server anywhere holding your data, because there is no NIDO server

What NIDO does, how it protects it, and a double challenge at the end.

The only servers the app ever contacts are public download sources, when you fetch a model or a knowledge pack, and every download is written into a network log inside the app that you can open and read.

The brain runs on the phone. You download your model once, and after that the internet can go away. The standard pick is Qwen2.5 with 1.5 billion parameters, or its 0.5 billion sibling on smaller phones. If your phone can carry more, you can step up to Phi-3.5, Qwen 7B, LFM or Gemma. All of them think locally, on your hardware, with the radios off if you want.

It remembers. Facts about you, your preferences, your people, your notes and your conversations live in a persistent memory on the device, and the assistant uses that memory when it answers. It also reads knowledge packs built from Wikipedia: a thousand topics, four thousand, or the fifty thousand Vital Articles, searchable offline. You can add your own documents too, plain text, spreadsheets and PDFs, and they stay on the phone.

It has hands. Twenty six local tools: notes, reminders on the system alarm, calendar events, contacts, calls and texts it can start for you, a calculator, a unit converter, your files, your tables. For anything sensitive it has to ask first. That is a rule in the code, not a promise in a brochure. It can also work while you sleep: scheduled tasks in plain words, like "every morning at 7, check my calendar and brief me". You can talk to it and it talks back, asking your phone for on device speech recognition. Today it speaks English, Spanish and Portuguese. More languages are being translated with native reviewers, and I will only claim them when they ship.

And it talks to other NIDO phones, directly, over Bluetooth or the same Wi-Fi network, with no server in the middle. Paired phones can chat, share knowledge packs, and even delegate tasks to each other with signed permission slips that are limited in scope and time, and that you approve or reject. Nobody unpaired gets a session.

Now the vault, because everything above sits inside it. Your memory, conversations and notes rest in an encrypted database, SQLCipher. The key that opens it is a random 32 byte key created on the phone, never derived from a PIN or anything predictable. And you can seal that key inside the phone itself: turn on hardware protection in the security settings, and the key is wrapped by a second key that is born inside your phone's security chip, StrongBox on the phones that carry one, and that never leaves it. From then on the vault only opens with your PIN, your pattern or your fingerprint, and the chip demands one of them every single time the key is used. There is even a maximum security mode on top: step away from the app for longer than the time you picked, thirty seconds to five minutes, and NIDO shuts down completely and wipes the key from memory. A biometric or PIN gate also stands in front of the app when it opens and when it comes back from the background. Backups are copies of that same encrypted database, and the key travels separately, in your hands: without it, the backup is a brick. If you wipe your data inside the app, it deletes the databases and the keys, hardware key included, and then it checks that nothing survived. On the wire, two phones shake hands with their identity keys, an X25519 key that names each phone and an Ed25519 key that signs for it, plus fresh temporary keys for every connection, and those temporary secrets are erased the moment the session key exists. Everything you then say to each other travels sealed. A listener nearby can tell that two phones are talking. The conversation itself is ciphertext to them.

I built NIDO for the places that need it most. The town where the power goes out. The country where the internet gets shut off on election day. The farm, the desert, the long road. The places where "just use the cloud" is a bad joke. Your voice should not depend on anyone's permission, or on anyone's electricity but your own.

I have looked hard for a hole in this. So far I have not found one. If you find something that breaks NIDO's security or its privacy, say it, in public or through the private report channel on the repo. I will fix it, and I will thank you for it.

And one more claim, so you can prove me wrong twice. I do not know of another app that even tries to put all of this in one place: an assistant that runs fully offline, a memory that remembers you, an encrypted vault, and encrypted phone to phone messaging and task sharing, with no cloud and no accounts. If it exists, show me.

Prove me wrong.

text:
My mutation test run killed 252 of 252 mutants. Every kill was fake.

I use Claude Code to build small Python tools that run parts of my home setup, and for anything that matters I have it mutation test the test suite: change the code on purpose, one small break at a time, and check that some test fails for each one. A mutant that no test notices is a hole in the tests.

The run that looked perfect: three hours, 252 mutants, 252 killed. Then the check I run after every long run failed. That check pushes the unchanged code through the same runner, and it should pass. It didnt.

What happened: the runner copies the code and the tests into a fresh temp folder for each mutant. Three days earlier a test had started reading a small data file that sits next to the code. Nobody added that file to the runner's copy list. So in every copy, mutated or not, that one test failed, and every mutant "died" of the same missing file. The runner's own baseline didn't catch it, because it ran on the source folder, where the file exists.

It was worse than one wasted morning. The same bug had already voided an earlier "11 of 11 killed" for a change I'd shipped, and that number was sitting in my change log as evidence. With the runner fixed, the 11 held up, and a full rerun of the 252 killed them all for real. But for three days that number proved nothing.

It wasn't the first time either. An earlier run crossed midnight with its test venv under /tmp. The venv lost its config file overnight (I think macOS's tmp cleanup got it), pytest couldn't start anymore, and a suite that can't start fails. So everything after midnight read as killed.

What I do now:

1. Every run has a control: a comment-only change that must survive. If the control dies, the run is void.

2. The control goes through the runner's own copy step, before and after the run. A baseline on the source folder hides a file the copy is missing.

3. "Killed" isn't evidence on its own. The log names the failing tests for each kill. If one test name shows up in every kill, thats not a strong suite, it's one broken test.

4. When a test starts reading a new file, the file goes on the copy list in the same change.

5. Long runs go through a wrapper that fingerprints the source folders before and after (names, sizes, hashes) and marks the run VOID if anything changed. Claude once added a test in the middle of a run, so the later mutants ran against different tests than the first ones.

If you run evals or an LLM judge, same idea: a case that has to pass and a case that has to fail, every run, through the exact same harness. 100% should make you suspicious, not happy.

text:
20 AI agents, hundreds of thousands of test executions, and I'm still figuring out how to keep them accountable

Figured I'd share an update on my multi-agent project. I've posted about the general architecture before, but things have progressed quite a bit.

I'm currently about halfway through the third major iteration. Running 20 agents with different responsibilities, a central coordinator, task dispatching, auditing, and a separate machine handling some supporting services.

The funny thing is, getting agents to actually do things isn't really my biggest problem anymore. It's proving they did what they claimed.

I've had tasks marked as verified when the application couldn't even launch. Agents reporting success despite failed checks. Retries duplicating work. Changes breaking unrelated systems. You name it.

At some point I realized adding more agents wasn't going to fix any of that.

So the latest iteration has been focused almost entirely on governance, accountability, and evidence.

Over the past couple of weeks, I've built out a hash-chained audit ledger, deterministic policy checks, action contracts, human approvals, evidence verification, and a separate validation process.

The whole thing is still running in shadow mode. It watches and evaluates what the agents are doing but doesn't automatically block them yet. I'm not giving it that authority until the evidence supports it.

Some numbers from the development records:

\- 20 agents in the fleet.

\- 6,111 recorded test runs.

\- 805,299 test case executions.

\- 4,525 runs performed by review agents, roughly 74% of recorded runs.

\- 19 recorded adversarial review rounds, with 648 findings across four packages.

\- 95.4% mutation kill rate from 5,133 scored mutants in that review snapshot.

\- An independent validator's first live run checked 3,267 records with zero findings.

\- A later validation checked 484 evidence artifacts with zero missing or mismatched.

\- 211 findings accounted for out of 211 in the latest manual triage.

To clarify, the cumulative testing numbers cover the broader development environment since late August, not just this version. They include repeated runs, intentional failures, and regression testing. Some of the review statistics are also older snapshots.

I'm not pretending 800k test executions means 800k different things were tested. Lol.

One of the more interesting moments was the first live pilot. Five actual development tickets went through the new system. Four effects were verified automatically. The fifth triggered a finding that turned out to be a problem with the verification logic itself.

So yeah, I now have a system that checks the agents, and another system checking parts of the system that checks the agents.

And even that isn't perfect.

Just recently we discovered some stale regression tests. The existing suite could pass while not actually testing everything we thought it was testing. That was a pretty good reminder that a green checkmark means absolutely nothing if the check itself is wrong.

I've also gotten much stricter about deployments. Written designs, multiple adversarial review rounds, mutation testing, frozen code snapshots, staged deployments, rollback procedures, and manual approval before production changes.

It's probably overkill for a personal project, but after seeing some of the earlier failures, I'd rather deal with the extra work.

For context, I'm not a professional software engineer. A lot of this has been built using AI-assisted development. I've learned a ridiculous amount just trying to understand why something broke, fixing it, and figuring out how to prevent it from happening again.

There's still a good bit left to implement, including stronger enforcement boundaries and a longer observation period. I'm not calling it finished or fully secure.

Eventually, I'd like to open-source some form of it, but that's a separate discussion.

The biggest lesson so far is that making AI agents useful and making AI agents accountable are two very different problems.

I feel to many projects lack on governance. I'm build from the inside out.

text:
Are we already overengineering AI agents?

A few days ago I asked about agents crashing halfway through a task: an external API creates a record, but the worker dies before saving the response. The replies helped sharpen something I'd been thinking about more broadly.

We can make two mistakes at once: add capabilities the task doesn't need, while leaving basic failure handling vague. A document classifier probably doesn't need a team of agents, long-term memory, a vector database, and an event bus. A single model call with validation might be easier to understand and evaluate. But an agent that changes records across several systems has different requirements. Some of the most useful suggestions in that thread were about recording intent and a stable operation ID before acting, then treating an unknown outcome as a state that needs reconciliation. 

One commenter described parking money or inventory operations for review, while allowing analytics calls to retry and deduplicating later. That was a useful reminder that recovery policy depends on what a duplicate would actually cost. Those mechanisms add complexity, but they address identifiable failures. Removing them can leave someone piecing together what happened after a crash. So the test I'd use for each component is: what specific requirement or failure does it address, and who owns it when it breaks? Memory needs a reason to retain information. Retrieval needs an information gap to fill. Multiple agents need a division of work that justifies the coordination. Execution history needs enough detail to support recovery. That's where I see the appeal of a runtime such as Diagrid Catalyst, which I mentioned in the earlier thread. Moving execution persistence into shared infrastructure can reduce what each application has to maintain. The tool and external service still need a clear contract for retries, duplicate protection, and uncertain outcomes.

A platform also introduces a dependency and a programming model to understand. I'd want to know which responsibilities it actually takes over and which remain with the application. I'd start with the smallest system I can evaluate, then add the operational guarantees its actions require.

What component have you removed that made your agent simpler without making it less dependable? And what looked unnecessary until a failure showed why you needed it?

Which non-coding agent workflows actually stuck at your company?

Coding agents get most of the attention. I'm curious about what holds up outside a codebase, where you often don't have a test suite telling you whether the job is actually done.

If your team uses agents for ops, finance, support, research, reporting, or other non-coding work, what's one workflow people still rely on after the initial excitement wore off? What does the agent actually do, how often does it run, and how long has it been in use? I'm more interested in work moving across systems than another email-drafting demo.

How do you keep the result reliable across runs? Not identical wording, but consistently finding the right records, applying the same rules, and producing something you can trust. What catches a plausible-looking wrong answer before someone acts on it, and when does a human step in?

I'm also curious how this spreads beyond whoever built it. Do you share prompts, SOPs, reusable workflows, example inputs and expected outputs? Can a teammate run it without the original builder standing behind them?

And what did the before/after actually look like? Time per task or per week is fine, but including review, corrections, maintenance, and tool costs—not just execution time. A rough estimate is useful; just say if it's measured or a guess.

If you tried this and went back to doing it manually or using a plain script, I'd like to hear that too. One concrete workflow and what went wrong would be more useful than a list of tools or a “10x productivity” claim.

We built a WhatsApp bot for an EA Sports FC campaign that could only say one thing. 15K conversations, +23% sales.

Everyone wants their bot to be smarter. For this one, the brief was basically the opposite.

Context: in January 2026, EA SPORTS FC 26 was free on Xbox for four days during Free Play Days. The goal was to get lapsed players off the old version and into the new one. 

Edelman, the agency running the campaign, came up with the idea of Toni Kroos personally inviting fans via a WhatsApp voice note. Our team at BotsCrew built and ran the conversational side.

The entire flow:

* A fan taps a link on IG, TikTok, YouTube, X, or the campaign site
* WhatsApp opens with a pre-filled message about a friend “still playing the old game,” and the fan hits send
* The bot replies instantly with Kroos’s voice note (his real recording, not a synthetic voice) and one CTA
* Anything sent after that gets one fixed reply

That’s it. The bot never joins groups. Every share comes from a real person forwarding the voice note.

Then the fun part. None of the hard problems were about the conversation:

* About 10 days to build, 4 days live. There was no second chance. A broken day one would have cost a quarter of the campaign.
* Ban risk. WhatsApp can suspend a fresh Business number within minutes when volume spikes, which is exactly what a viral campaign is designed to cause. We flagged this to the client before kickoff, along with what we’d do if it happened.
* Bursty traffic with no warm-up. We ran stress and load tests against WhatsApp’s incoming message limits well before launch. On the day, the platform scaled to six instances and didn’t drop a single reply.
* Tracking. Each channel got its own Bitly deep link, so the click is logged before WhatsApp even opens. Voice-note delivery is confirmed via a tracked API call, and a second tracked link in the CTA shows who actually visited the landing page.

We reused an existing platform running in production instead of building from scratch. That’s the main reason the build came in about 25% under the estimated effort, and the saved time went into analytics and launch coordination.

Results:

* 15K unique conversations
* Up to \~40% conversion to the game
* \+23% sales uplift
* 8.2M organic views across the campaign

The glamorous part was a voice note from Toni Kroos. The rest were rate limits, load scripts, and a backup plan for WhatsApp flagging the number.

text:
If you lock the tests your agent is judged against, what stops it changing what runs them?

Most of the protections I see described here are directory-shaped: block writes to tests/`,` mount the acceptance suite read-only, keep a second set the agent can’t see, run the base-commit tests regardless of what’s in the working tree.

I went looking for what gets past that. Two things did, and neither touches a test file.

A newly created conftest .py at the repo root. A changed pytest.ini. Collection changes underneath the tests you protected, the assertions you wrote never execute, and pytest still exits 0. If your gate reads the exit code (&& most do) that run is indistinguishable from a real pass.

Blocking writes to tests/ catches neither, because neither lives in tests/. The file that decides what runs usually isn’t the file you’re protecting.

What I landed on is treating whatever controls collection as part of the surface being verified, rather than scaffolding around it. That closes those two. I don’t think it closes everything.

So: if you’ve locked down the suite your agent is judged against, **what’s the hole you already know about and haven’t fixed?** I’d rather hear the ones you’re living with than the clean designs.

And a harder one I haven’t solved. Protections like this produce holds, and some of them are noise. A hold that turns out to be nothing costs the same attention as one that matters & once people stop reading holds, the whole thing is theatre. How do you keep the false-hold rate low enough that people keep reading them? Or do you just accept it and move the threshold?

text:
An agent deleted our lead lists, so I set out to replace Postgres. Here’s what I built instead (first release)

A few weeks ago an AI agent with write access to our CRM deleted all our lead lists. It needed write access to do its job, so “make it read-only” wasn’t an answer.

My plan was to replace Postgres: a new database where every agent run writes to its own branch, you see exactly what it changed, row by row, and you decide what merges back. I posted about it here and asked what you’d need to trust it.

Two answers changed everything:

1. **“The branch is the easy part. The merge is what has to be trusted.”** Branching a database is solved; Neon and others do it in seconds. Nobody had a merge back into production you’d trust.
2. **“I’m not moving my CRM to a new database for this.”** Almost everyone said a version of this. Fair.

So the first release does the opposite of my plan. It sits **beside** the Postgres you already run. It copies the tables your agent works on, each run gets its own branch of them, and when the agent merges, the change is written back to your Postgres in one transaction, but only after:

* checking every row it changes is still as it was when the agent started (someone else changed it meanwhile? conflict, nothing written);
* checking that rows the agent *read* haven’t changed either (it decided on facts that are gone);
* running your SQL checks against the merged result (two changes fine alone, wrong together);
* applying your rules: no deletes without a person, max rows, tables that always need review. Limits count across the whole run, so splitting a delete into small pieces doesn’t get around them.

If a rule says no, the merge waits for you, with the reasons, and Postgres hasn’t been touched.

Things I learned building it:

* The hard part was never the branch. It was making “is this row still the same?” never give a false alarm across timezones, float formats and triggers. The fix was to let Postgres itself do the comparing.
* Serial ids are a trap: an agent inserting rows in a copy will collide with your app later. It now reserves ids from your own sequence.
* Connection poolers (PgBouncer in transaction mode) quietly break anything that relies on session state. Every setting has to be per-transaction.

Honest status: first release, a beta, for staging copies. I’m one person, and nobody outside me has run a real agent on it yet.

**Question for people whose agents write to a database today:** what do you do now, read-only, direct writes, or something in between? And what would you need to see before letting an agent merge into production without you watching?

text:
Grok Bot: what's eating all my usage?! I priced a week of usage call by call. Long jobs were 52% of the cost.

I blew through more Grok Bot usage than I care to admit. Got hooked on bots and wanted to keep working with them, so I had to keep upping the ante!

- Started on the free plan Sunday and ran out the same day
- $20 plan got me 3 more days
- $60 plan got me 2 more days
- Added $20 of extra usage and that went by in 90 minutes
- By 9 PM Friday I was on the $200 plan, five days after starting on the free one, and I couldn't tell you where the money went. So I spent the weekend finding out: every call in the usage export, priced at list API rates.

**TL;DR**

- **What it cost:** the plan went from $20 to $200 a month in five days.
- **Why:** long multi-step jobs. Runs of 16 steps or more were 52% of the cost.
- **What to do:** decide where a job runs before it starts, script what repeats, hand long jobs to Cursor, and talk to the bot that does the work.

*Note: this analysis was done on the Cursor plan before the unified X plan came out, so some things may be a bit different now. Good chance Grok Bot is still burning usage, and because it shares quota with Cursor, it's unclear that shifting tasks to Cursor will help.*

**The bill.**

| Date | Plan | What happened |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sun Oct 4 | Free | Ran out during a Sunday workshop |
| Sun Oct 4 | $20/month | Ran out around Wednesday |
| Wed Oct 7 | $60/month | Ran out Friday at 4:48 PM |
| Fri Oct 9 | $20 extra usage | Gone in about 90 minutes. $20.13 billed |
| Fri Oct 9 | $200/month | Moved up at about 9 PM |
| Mon Oct 12 | $30, X's unified plan | Switched, and the $200 plan was refunded |

**Where it went.**

- **Long jobs.** 117 runs of 16 steps or more cost $323, 52% of the week. A quick question costs a few re-reads. "Go through these files and update the plan" costs a re-read on every step, and the re-reads grow as the job goes on.
- **The front door.** The chief of staff bot takes every request first, so it carries the longest history. It cost $236 for October 6 to 12, twice as much as any other bot. Its most expensive single job coordinated several bots, ran 222 steps and cost $15.31.
- **Full reloads.** 248 calls loaded 50,000 tokens or more with nothing cached. They added $69.
- **Small asks.** Five one-line spoken edits to one short email cost $1.26. About $1.10 of that was re-reading a 120,000-token chat.
- **Scheduled jobs** looked like the obvious suspect. They were about 8% of the cost.

**Why.** About 90% of the tokens were re-reads of context the bot already had. Every agent works this way, so that share is normal. What makes it expensive is how long the history gets and how many steps a job takes. A blank bot loaded 34,868 tokens on its first reply. The chief of staff bot was carrying 168,709, about 80% of it its own history, memory and job description. A new chat did not reset it, because every chat on a bot shares one context. Re-read pricing also differs: Grok 4.7 charges a quarter of its input price for cached tokens, and Claude Opus 5.5 charges a twentieth.

**Why the bot won't fix it.** There is no step limit or max-steps setting in the docs. Staff on the vendor's forum say chat instructions are "only a hint they can ignore," and this setup had a written rule to hand off long jobs that the bots still broke 117 times. No tool shows a bot what it has spent. The plans page says "a limit is not a hard stop in the middle of a run." Every control that works sits outside the bot.

**What to do.**

1. **Measure first.** Download the usage file, price it at published rates and sort calls by job length. The guess here was scheduled jobs, and the guess was wrong.
2. **Script what repeats.** A script on a schedule has no conversation to re-read.
3. **Hand long jobs off before they start.** Send them to a separate agent with a clean page (a cloud agent, Codex or Claude Code) and have the bot read the result from a file. A helper inside the same bot costs the same per call as the main chat ($0.063 against $0.061).
4. **Talk to the bot that does the work.** Routing through a chief of staff bot means two long histories get re-read.
5. **Pass work by file.** One bot writes the request to a shared file, and the next reads only that file.
6. **Compare re-read prices** when you compare tools.

**Sanity check on the platform.** In a same-job test, a blank Grok bot did three small jobs for less than half of what Claude Code (Opus 5.5) cost, and about a fifth on two of them. The models differ too, so treat this as a sanity check. Long histories and long jobs drove the bill.

**How it was measured.** The vendor's usage export, one row per call, in a small SQLite pipeline. Grok 4.7 list rates: $2 per million input tokens, $0.50 cache reads, $6 output, with cache writes priced like input since no separate rate is listed. 33 calls on 8 other models had no published rate, so totals are floors. Calls are grouped into one run until they go quiet for more than 45 seconds. Per-bot figures cover October 6 to 12 (about $634); the rest cover October 4 to 11.

The day-to-day bots have since moved to Muse's $16 Power plan. The multipliers moved with them, and a larger allowance only makes them cheaper.

I completed 2 technical audits, got real results, and still have 0 paying clients. Here's what I'm learning.

​

I've been building a small technical consulting business around independent RAG retrieval evaluations.

The technical side has gone better than the commercial side.

I've completed two audit cases. In one of them, I identified 15 scoring discrepancies in an open-source RAG benchmark. The project's maintainer independently reproduced the findings and incorporated corrections.

That gave me something valuable: evidence that the work can produce useful technical results.

I packaged the service into a fixed $400 assessment, comparing two existing retrieval configurations across up to 30 selected queries, with reproducible findings.

Then I started looking for customers.

I tried reaching people working on RAG systems, participating in technical discussions, and researching companies that might need independent evaluations.

Here's what surprised me.

Technical interest and buying intent are completely different things.

People will discuss retrieval quality, evaluation metrics, and regressions. Some genuinely appreciate the work.

But that doesn't mean they have a reason to pay an external auditor.

I also researched competing services. Several providers advertise standalone technical assessments, but finding verifiable evidence of how they acquire paying clients is surprisingly difficult.

My current hypothesis is that customers don't necessarily buy an "audit." They buy help making a specific decision — whether to deploy a change, accept a vendor's work, or investigate a costly regression.

So I've paused cold outreach to better understand the actual buying process.

For those who have sold specialized B2B services like technical audits, QA, security assessments, or independent evaluations: where did your first paying client come from, and what made them pay for an assessment instead of handling it internally?

I'm especially interested in firsthand experiences, including cases where the business model didn't work.

I'm still at zero paid clients, so I'm sharing the learning process rather than pretending I've figured out the sales side.
